result.summary: The Trojans leave their chariots at the trench and attack the Achaean wall on foot. Despite an ill omen read by Polydamas and Hector's scorn for it, they press on, and Sarpedon breaks a breach in the battlements. Hector, aided by Jove, smashes the gates with a huge stone and leaps inside as the Danaans flee to their ships.

scenes.title: The wall's fate foretold
scenes.summary: The narrator explains that the unsanctioned wall will one day be washed away by Neptune and Apollo, then returns to the fighting around it.
scenes.stakes: The Achaeans' ships are threatened because the wall was built without offerings to the gods.

scenes.title: Polydamas advises fighting on foot
scenes.summary: Horses cannot cross the trench, so Polydamas urges the Trojans to dismount. Hector agrees and the army forms five companies.
scenes.stakes: The Trojans risk being trapped at the trench if the Achaeans rally.

place.name: the trench before the Achaean wall

scenes.title: Asius at the gates
scenes.summary: Asius drives his chariot to the open gates, where the Lapithae Polypoetes and Leonteus hold firm and kill many Trojans.
scenes.stakes: Asius faces death at the gates; the defenders protect the ships.

place.name: the gates on the left wing of the wall

scenes.title: The eagle and snake omen
scenes.summary: A snake drops from an eagle's talons among the Trojans. Polydamas reads it as a warning, but Hector rejects it and leads the attack.
scenes.stakes: Trojans risk heavy losses if they ignore the omen; Polydamas risks Hector's wrath.

scenes.title: The Ajaxes rally the defenders
scenes.summary: The Trojans tear at the battlements while the two Ajaxes cheer the Achaeans. Jove sets Sarpedon on them like a lion.
scenes.stakes: The Achaeans risk the wall falling and the ships being reached.

scenes.title: Sarpedon's speech to Glaucus
scenes.summary: Sarpedon argues that Lycian honours demand they lead the fight, since death comes to all.
scenes.stakes: Their glory and honour, and their lives in battle.

scenes.title: Menestheus calls for help
scenes.summary: Menestheus sends Thootes to fetch Ajax. Ajax and Teucer arrive and kill Epicles and wound Glaucus, but Sarpedon tears a breach in the battlement.
scenes.stakes: Menestheus's section of wall may fall to the Lycians.

scenes.title: A balanced struggle
scenes.summary: Sarpedon rallies the Lycians, and the fight hangs evenly until Jove favours Hector.
scenes.stakes: Control of the wall and access to the ships.

scenes.title: Hector breaks the gates
scenes.summary: Hector lifts a huge stone and smashes the gates open. He leaps in and the Trojans pour over the wall as the Danaans flee.
scenes.stakes: The Achaean ships are about to be burned and the army destroyed.

place.name: the gates of the Achaean wall

alias_notes.explanation: Phoebus is a common epithet of Apollo.
Jove is called son of scheming Saturn.
Distinguishes him from the other Ajax.

notable_quotes.reason: Hector's famous line that the only omen is fighting for one's country.
Sarpedon's reflection that death is unavoidable, so seek glory.
Asius accuses Jove of deceit when the Achaeans hold firm.

analysis.text: Hector's defiance of the omen shows rash confidence and the tension between divine signs and human resolve. Jove's favour carries him toward later ruin.
The wall built without hecatombs reflects the Greek belief that undertakings needed sacrifice and divine consent. Its destruction is also an etiological tale explaining the lack of ruins at Troy.

legacy.text: Hector's line that the best omen is to fight for one's country became a widely quoted patriotic saying.
Sarpedon's speech on noble obligation was admired and echoed by later writers as a statement of aristocratic duty.

fun_facts.text: The destruction of the wall by rivers and sea in sentences 4-7 is a rare passage where the poet looks past the end of the war.

language_notes.text: The son of Menoetius is Patroclus, who is tending the wounded Eurypylus in Achilles' hut, a task that leads him toward his fate.
Hecatombs were large sacrifices of cattle, originally a hundred oxen, offered to win the gods' favor.
The city was sacked in the tenth year: the story of Troy's fall lies outside the Iliad, and the narrator looks ahead to it here.
"Minister of Rout" means Hector is the agent or servant of Rout, the personified panic that drives armies to flight.
"Bitten the dust" here means fallen dead in battle.
Danaans is another name for the Greeks, like Argives and Achaeans.
An esquire is an attendant who looks after a warrior's horses and equipment; here he is the same as a charioteer.
"Ill-omened name" means a death of evil reputation; the sentence refers to Asius, who will die at Idomeneus' hands, as the narrator announces beforehand.
The Lapithae were a Thessalian people famed in myth for fighting the Centaurs; Pirithous, father of Polypoetes, was their king.
"Danaans" is another name for the Greeks, like Achaeans and Argives.
Smiting one's thighs is a Homeric gesture of shock, grief or anger.
Asius accuses Jove of lying because he had trusted that the Greeks would not hold out; he feels deceived.
"Girdle" here means the belt worn around the waist over the armour.
"Essayed" means attempted or tried; the youths had tried to cross the trench when the sign appeared.
"Forsooth" is an archaic word meaning "in truth," here used sarcastically to mock Hector's attitude.
"Danaans" is one of Homer's names for the Greeks, as are Achaeans and Argives.
"I like not of your reading" means "I do not like your interpretation."
Refers to Jove's earlier promise, in which he bowed his head to confirm that Hector would win glory at the ships.
Greeks read birds' flight by direction; omens on the right were usually favourable, on the left unfavourable. Hector dismisses this.
Danaans is another name for the Greeks, like Argives and Achaeans; Homer uses all three interchangeably.
"Good bad and indifferent" means brave, cowardly and middling; the Ajaxes admit men differ in prowess yet call on everyone.
"Vouchsafe" means to grant graciously; here the Ajaxes hope Jove will allow them to drive the Trojans back.
"These his arrows" calls snowflakes Jove's weapons, which he shows to mankind as a display of power.
"Fain" means eager or willing; Sarpedon is keen to attack the wall.
"Eat the fat of the land" means enjoy the best produce; the Lycians justify privilege by service in battle.
"The two Ajaxes" refers to Ajax son of Telamon (Great Ajax) and Ajax son of Oileus, two different heroes who often fought side by side.
"It will be all over with us" means the defenders will be destroyed; "directly" means very soon.
"Argives" is one of Homer's names for the Greeks as a whole, like Achaeans and Danaans.
"By the same father" marks Teucer as Ajax's half-brother; their mothers differed, though both were sons of Telamon.
"As men now are" is the narrator's typical contrast between the stronger heroes of old and weaker men of his own day.
"Covertly" means secretly; Glaucus hides his wound so the Achaeans will not see it and mock him.
"The ships' sterns" refers to the Greek ships drawn up behind the wall; Jove does not want his son Sarpedon to die there.
"Thus fail me" means to let him down by not supporting him; Sarpedon is the speaker, and he is a Lycian leader.
"Stickle" means to argue stubbornly over a point, here over very small claims to land.
"Rout" means to put to disorderly flight.
"As men now are" is the narrator's aside that heroes of the past were stronger than people of his own day.
"Cross-bars" are the bolts that held the double doors shut from inside; the single key probably worked the fastening.
"Portals" are the gates or doorways.

context_notes.text: Neptune (the Greek Poseidon) is god of the sea. Apollo supports Troy. The Scamander and Simois are rivers near Troy.
The Hellespont is the strait now called the Dardanelles, near Troy.
Paris is the Trojan prince whose abduction of Helen caused the war. Helenus and Deiphobus are his brothers.
Sarpedon, son of Jove, leads the Lycian allies of Troy.
The Greek wall and gates were built to protect the ships; the open gates let fleeing Greeks in.
Mars (the Greek Ares) is the god of war, so "peer of Mars" praises Leonteus as a fighter.
Jove had promised Thetis to give Hector glory until the Greeks honoured Achilles, so Asius's prayer cannot sway him.
Polydamas is a Trojan commander and Hector's companion, known for cautious counsel that Hector often overrides.
The aegis was Jove's storm-shield; "aegis-bearing" is his standing epithet.
Mount Ida near Troy is where Jove often sits to watch the battle.
Sarpedon, son of Jove, leads the Lycians, allies of Troy. Glaucus is his companion and fellow commander.
Sarpedon speaks of heroic reciprocity: nobles receive honours and land from their people and must repay them by leading in battle.
The Xanthus is the principal river of Lycia, in southern Asia Minor; the estate was a grant of land given to the princes.
Menestheus is an Athenian leader. The Greeks have built a wall to protect their ships, and the Trojans and their allies are now attacking it.
The Lycians are Trojan allies, led by Sarpedon and Glaucus, who are fighting at this section of the wall.
Teucer is Ajax's half-brother and the Greeks' best archer; he often shoots from behind Ajax's shield.
Sarpedon is a son of Jove (the Greek Zeus) by a mortal woman, so Jove protects him here.
Sarpedon, son of Jove, leads the Lycians, who are allies fighting for Troy.
Argives, Danaans and Achaeans are all names for the Greeks in this translation.
Saturn is the father of Jove (the Greek Zeus), who here favours Hector and helps him by divine power.

literary_notes.text: The lack of divine consent signals that the wall is doomed, and it frames the Greeks' defense as fragile.
The narrator steps out of the story to look ahead, then returns to the battle with an abrupt shift of tense.
Hector is compared to a lion or boar facing hunters. His courage is admirable but the simile hints that it will destroy him.
Asius' foolhardy refusal to dismount hints that he will meet a bad end.
The narrator tells us the Trojans' confidence is misplaced, as they will meet two stubborn champions at the gates.
The defenders are compared to oaks that endure wind and rain, stressing their steadfastness and deep rootedness.
The two defenders are compared to wild boars standing against men and dogs, adding ferocity and a hint of eventual doom.
Missiles falling like thick snowflakes conveys the density and endlessness of the barrage.
Wasps and bees defending their nests illustrate how small defenders can fiercely guard their homes.
The poet interrupts to admit he is no god, a modest nod to the Muses as source of knowledge.
The wounded eagle dropping its prey previews the Trojans' coming failure to carry off their gains.
The eagle and snake stand for the Trojans and Achaeans; the dropped prey signals a costly, failed assault.
Hector's scornful question dismisses omens entirely and shows his confidence.
Hector's famous line shows his patriotic courage and also his stubborn refusal to heed warnings.
Jove helps the Trojans, but this encourages the rash confidence that will lead to their losses, as the omen warned.
The falling stones are compared to a heavy, silent snowfall burying mountains and fields, conveying the overwhelming density of missiles.
Sarpedon is likened to a starving lion breaking into a fold, stressing his hunger for battle and fearless determination.
The lion's choice between taking a sheep or being speared hints that Sarpedon's attack may bring either victory or death.
Sarpedon's reasoning shows him as a thoughtful hero who accepts mortality and chooses glory because death cannot be avoided.
The Lycians storming the battlements are compared to a thick dark cloud, conveying their number and the threat they pose.
The stone is so heavy that even a strong young man could hardly lift it, which magnifies Ajax's superhuman strength.
Epicles falls "as though he were diving," a grim comparison that makes his lifeless fall look almost graceful.
Sarpedon's tearing down the battlement with his bare hands shows his strength and determination, and he is the first to breach the wall.
The struggle over the battlements is compared to a petty boundary quarrel, making the fierce fight seem stubborn and evenly matched.
The honest working woman's scales stand for the evenly balanced battle, and her poverty adds a humble, human tone to the war.
The shepherd easily lifting a fleece shows how light the stone feels to Hector, stressing Jove's help.
Hector's dark face is likened to night, making him look terrifying and almost supernatural.
Saying only a god could withstand him stresses Hector's overwhelming power at this moment.
